chunks: Jitter. The question: What is jitter?
Jitter is how much the edges of a signal arrive earlier or later than they should. A 100 megahertz clock should have an edge every 10 nanoseconds exactly.
In reality each edge is off by a tiny amount, often a few picoseconds (1 picoseconds is a trillionth of a second). Jitter eats into the time a receiver has to capture data.
Picture a drummer playing along with a metronome. A perfect drummer hits exactly on every click.
A real drummer is a little early or late on each hit, and the errors differ from beat to beat. The timing errors are the jitter.
If the band needs every hit inside a short window, big errors miss it. Some errors are random. Others repeat, such as always rushing after a rest.
Edge positions drift from their ideal grid (the jitter here is exaggerated to 1. 5 nanoseconds, with a slow 37 nanoseconds wander).
The shift of any single edge is its TIE; the variation in spacing between neighboring edges is period jitter.
Jitter: the difference between when an edge happens and when it should have happened. Unit interval (UI): the time of one bit. At 10 Gb/s it is 100 picoseconds.
Slew rate: how fast the voltage changes during an edge, in volts per ns. Random vs. deterministic jitter: random comes from noise and is unpredictable.
Deterministic repeats and has a cause, such as crosstalk or the data pattern.
Setup and hold margin: the spare timing a receiver has around its sampling moment ("Setup and hold times (SI view)").
A 3. 3 volts edge takes 1 nanoseconds to rise, so its slope is about 2. 64 volts/ns. Add 15 millivolts of random noise right at the receiver's switching point.
The edge crosses that point earlier or later by 15 millivolts / 2. 64 volts/ns, about 5. 7 picoseconds. On a 10 Gb/s link, one bit lasts 100 picoseconds.
So this one noise source alone eats about 6% of the bit time. That is the whole idea: noise at the switching point turns into timing error.
"Jitter is the deviation of edges from their ideal time positions.
It's measured as period jitter, cycle-to-cycle jitter, or TIE against an ideal clock, and split into random jitter, which is Gaussian, and deterministic jitter, which is bounded.
It comes from noise converted at the threshold, supply and ground noise, crosstalk, ISI, and oscillator phase noise.
It matters because it eats setup and hold margin, limits ADC SNR, and closes the eye so BER goes up."
